mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Sunday, August 23, 2026. Harvard Business School has integrated artificial intelligence avatars into its $699 HBS Foundry entrepreneurship bootcamp to provide students with feedback. Created by the startup HeyGen, these digital personas are designed to critique practice pitches and board meeting simulations. While the program maintains weekly live sessions with human instructors, the avatars handle routine feedback tasks. Early feedback from participants suggests a positive reception, even as some describe the digital likenesses as occasionally uncanny. The project serves as a test case for how educational institutions can use AI to scale personalized instruction, shifting the technology’s role from a simple chatbot to a more guided, interactive participant in the learning process. This development is significant because it explores how high-touch academic environments can leverage automation to handle repetitive assessment tasks without sacrificing student engagement. In infrastructure developments, Amazon Web Services detailed a method to reduce the costs of Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG, on Amazon Bedrock. RAG is a technique that gives AI models access to external data to improve the accuracy of their responses. However, because it involves sending large amounts of retrieved data to a model, it can become expensive and computationally heavy. Amazon’s proposed query-aware compression uses a smaller, lower-cost model to filter retrieved information before it reaches the primary model. By removing irrelevant context, companies can lower input token counts—the units of data processed by the model—thereby reducing costs and potentially decreasing the risk of hallucinations, where an AI generates incorrect or fabricated information. This approach is particularly important for enterprise-scale operations where costs scale linearly with the volume of tokens processed. Separately, London-based startup Inherent, founded by former Google DeepMind employees, announced the release of Faraday, an AI agent capable of independently replicating scientific research findings. Inherent reports that Faraday outperformed much larger systems from Anthropic and OpenAI in reproduction tasks while running on a smaller 27-billion-parameter model. The company aims to develop agents that possess research taste—the ability to determine which experiments are worth pursuing. By utilizing reinforcement learning, a training method that rewards systems for reaching desired outcomes rather than following strict rules, the company hopes to create agents that act more like collaborative scientific teammates than simple search tools. This signifies a move toward autonomous agents that can prioritize high-value research directions, potentially accelerating discovery timelines by reducing the need for constant manual oversight. In developer ecosystem news, Hugging Face recently released LFM2.5-DSpark, a tool designed to accelerate AI inference—the process of a model generating a response—by up to 3.2 times. The technology uses a technique called speculative decoding, where a smaller, faster draft model generates candidate tokens that a larger target model then verifies. This method significantly reduces the time spent waiting for hardware to process data, particularly on consumer hardware like the M4 Max MacBook Pro. The project also provides support for the llama.cpp and SGLang environments, making these speed improvements accessible to a broader range of developers. Such advancements are crucial for bringing agentic AI capabilities to edge devices, allowing more complex models to run locally without the latency inherent in cloud-based API calls. Finally, Panasonic Avionics Corporation has partnered with AWS to apply agentic AI to the diagnostics of in-flight entertainment and connectivity systems. By automating the analysis of logs and performance metrics across their global fleet, the company aims to reduce the time engineers spend manually correlating data to identify system issues. This move is part of a broader industry shift toward using AI to streamline complex maintenance workflows that previously required deep institutional knowledge and significant manual oversight. The collaboration aims to improve Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Resolve metrics, allowing engineering talent to shift focus from reactive troubleshooting toward long-term system reliability.
